summary: Learners aged 13–14 compose a full structured science report (aim, hypothesis, method, results, conclusion, evaluation) in objective scientific register, and come to understand WHY science is reported this way: peer review and independent replication are the social mechanisms that make scientific knowledge trustworthy. The load-bearing skill is extended scientific writing with reproducible methods and evidence-tied conclusions; the nature-of-science half is understanding that reliability comes from independent scrutiny, not authority.
misconceptions: Writing the method as a past-tense story rather than a reproducible procedure.
Writing a conclusion that restates the hypothesis without citing the actual data.
Treating the evaluation as an afterthought instead of a genuine analysis of reliability and error.
Believing peer review proves a result is TRUE, rather than that it has passed expert scrutiny.
Thinking a single study settles a question, overlooking the role of independent replication.
Using casual, first-person or overclaiming language instead of objective scientific register.
Omitting units/significant figures in the results as if presentation were separate from rigour.

activities.title: Report studio: compose the six sections with built-in checks
steps: Write a complete report with the conventional sections — aim, testable hypothesis, method, results, conclusion, evaluation — for an investigation you have actually run or been given full data for.
Draft the method as a numbered, unambiguous procedure that states what was kept constant (controlled variables), not as a past-tense story of what you did.
Build results tables and graphs with headed columns, SI units and correct significant figures throughout.
Write a conclusion that quotes specific values, a gradient, or a trend from your own data and states whether it supports the hypothesis — do not merely restate the hypothesis.
Write an evaluation that genuinely analyses reliability: identify anomalies, distinguish systematic from random error, and propose specific improvements.
Before finalising, check each section against stated success criteria for that section.
activities.insight: A scientific report is not a diary of what happened; each section has a distinct job, and together they present evidence and reasoning precisely enough for others to scrutinise.

activities.title: The reproducibility test: hand your method to someone else
steps: Give your written method — and ONLY the written text, not your verbal explanation — to a partner (or a simulated replicator) who tries to carry out the experiment following exactly what is written.
Observe where the replicator stalls, guesses, or does something different because an instruction was vague (e.g. 'heat it for a while', 'add some water').
Note every point where their result diverged from yours and check whether it can be traced to an ambiguous sentence (some differences may instead come from random variation or different equipment).
Rewrite each ambiguous step so a stranger would perform it identically, then have them try again.
activities.insight: A report must be a set of instructions precise enough for someone else to repeat and check you. Watching a reader fail to reproduce your result because of a fuzzy sentence shows why science demands reproducible methods.

activities.title: Review desk: critique a flawed report against criteria
steps: Read a sample report containing deliberate flaws (a vague method, an overreaching conclusion, an unsupported claim, a missing control, missing units).
Mark each weakness and explain against explicit criteria why it fails — e.g. 'this conclusion claims more than the data shows', 'this method cannot be reproduced because…'.
Compare a gold-standard report and a flawed one section by section, articulating what makes each section strong or weak.
Suggest the specific revision each flaw requires.
activities.insight: Peer review chiefly scrutinises method, evidence, and reasoning — whether the conclusions are actually justified — rather than spelling or formatting. Learning to spot overreach and vagueness in others' work sharpens it in your own.

activities.title: Why peer review and replication make knowledge reliable
steps: Respond to the prompt: 'A scientist publishes a surprising result. Before other scientists accept it, the work goes through peer review, and other labs try to replicate it. Why aren't the scientist's own careful report and honest word enough — what do peer review and independent replication add? And what would it mean if no one else could reproduce the result?'

In a role-play, defend your own report to a reviewer/editor who probes: 'Is your method reproducible? Does your conclusion overreach the data? What would a replication need?' Then swap seats and review the character's flawed manuscript.

Argue through the discriminating cases: What does a reviewer check that the original scientist might have missed? If three other labs get a different result, what should happen to the claim? Does a scientist being famous and careful make replication unnecessary? Why is a result only one lab can ever produce treated with suspicion?
activities.insight: Reliability comes from independent scrutiny and reproduction by OTHER labs — not from the authority, fame, or honesty of the scientist. A result earns trust only when others independently obtain it; failure to replicate is grounds to doubt the claim. All scientific knowledge stays provisional: independent confirmation makes us more confident in a claim, but later evidence can still revise or overturn it.

activities.title: Check component knowledge of conventions and nature of science
steps: Match each piece of content to the report section it belongs in (e.g. 'what was kept constant' → method; 'the gradient of the weight–mass graph was 9.8 N/kg' → results/conclusion).
Put the sections of a report into the correct order.
Identify the purpose of peer review and of replication from short options, distinguishing scrutiny of reasoning from proofreading.
Spot the weakness in a short sample method or conclusion snippet (e.g. a conclusion that cites no data).
activities.insight: The conventions of report structure and the facts about peer review and replication can be checked quickly, but they are prerequisites for — not a substitute for — actually composing and defending a report.

checkQuestion: A scientist publishes a surprising result. Before other scientists accept it, the work goes through peer review, and other labs try to replicate it. Why aren't the scientist's own careful report and honest word enough — what do peer review and independent replication add that makes a claim trustworthy? And what would it mean if no one else could reproduce the result?
checkAnswer: A strong response explains that peer review has independent experts scrutinise the method and reasoning for flaws or overclaiming before publication, and that replication by OTHER labs guards against mistakes, bias, flukes, or fraud the original team might not catch — a result earns trust only when others, independently, get it too. If no one can reproduce it, the claim is doubted (it may have been a one-off, an error, or an artefact of that lab), and the knowledge is treated as provisional until confirmed. It locates reliability in independent scrutiny, not authority.
